newsitem.title: BURMA: KNU says Burma aided in attack on refugee camps.
newsitem.headline: KNU says Burma aided in attack on refugee camps.

text.p: The leader of the Karen National Union (KNU) guerrilla organisation on Friday accused the Burmese government of being involved in attacks on three Karen refugee camps in Thailand earlier this week.

Earlier on Friday, Burma's military government said the Democratic Karen Buddhist Army (DKBA), a breakaway faction of the ethnic Karen group supported by Rangoon, was behind the attacks in which at least three people died.

"The Burmese soldiers were collaborating and joined operations with the DKBA (Democratic Karen Buddhist Army) in attacking and burning down refugee camps inside Thailand," the self-proclaimed general said at a gathering of about 500 guerrillas and about 1,000 Karen civilians.

General Bo Mya, president of the KNU -- one of the world's oldest rebel organisations -- also reaffirmed the KNU's vow to continue its armed struggle against Burma's military regime, saying the latest round of peace talks had failed.
Bo Mya made the comments to reporters during celebrations to mark the 48th anniversary of Karen Revolution Day in this camp in Burma's eastern jungles near the Thai border.
He said Burmese soldiers were among the group of armed men that torched three camps housing about 26,000 Karen refugees just inside Thailand after armed rebels made separate raids on the camps.
Three people were killed and thousands left homeless from the attacks, Thai police said.
A statement issued by Burma's ruling State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC) and obtained by Reuters on Friday said the DKBA was responsible for the attacks.
It said the raid was a retaliatory act because members of the KNU had entered Burma from Thailand in December and killed six people in an attack on a DKBA village.
The DKBA was formed in 1995 after a mutiny within the predominantly Christian KNU.
DKBA soldiers have since crossed into Thailand and attacked camps housing about 70,000 refugees several times, killing or wounding scores of refugees or KNU members.
Thai border police said on Friday the Thai army had reinforced the border area and sent planes to bomb jungle areas on the bank of the Moei River which divides the two countries.
Bo Mya said the KNU, which was formed in 1948 to fight for autonomy from Rangoon, would continue to fight the SLORC.
"Since our previous peace effort failed to make progress the KNU will continue its armed struggle against the SLORC," he said.
Representatives from the KNU and SLORC have met several times but failed to reach any agreement.

Early this month, senior Burmese government officials said they wanted to hold a new round of peace talks with the KNU -- the last major ethnic rebel group yet to sign a ceasefire agreement with the SLORC.
Bo Mya also predicted other rebel factions who have signed ceasefire agreements with the SLORC would resume fighting.
"During the meeting (of rebel groups) last month the delegates from the revolutionary groups said they will revoke the ceasefire and resume fighting in the near future," he said.
